title: The Savoy Male and Female College
text:

During my early childhood we lived in various towns in North Texas, where my father worked first as a store clerk, then as a teacher of literary schools and of special schools in penmanship, until his health failed. My mother also taught a private school in Celeste, Texas; and later—when I was perhaps ten—for a time in Galveston, where I had a hilarious time jumping into the in-rolling waves down on the beach.

My first school experience was in the winter of 1871-872, in Whitewright, where there was rather good subscription school. Later there were schools, many of which were taught by my father, but it was in 1878, while we were living in Mount Pleasant (a little village on a branch of the L. & A. railroad), that I began to experience my first real thirst for knowledge. Up to that time I did not know that the field of learning extended beyond the "three R's." The school at Custer City employed a real teacher, a University of Virginia graduate, B. F. Dean, who was reputed to have it that he could teach Greek, Latin, algebra, geometry, philosophy, logic, and what not. A well-meaning people, the Goldsmith, wondered how one small head could hold all he was reported to know. He came and I went to school to him—and was electrified after only six weeks info. Although I had never seen a Latin book, I persuaded him to read with me the Latin, and in the spring of the year I had thirty-two scholars in the Latin class of students from twenty to twenty-five years of age. He was a great teacher; on one occasion when I was with him I was reading Roman history. In order to give me a little help the first day I took the book he called for the story of the founding of Rome and the careers of Romulus and Remus; and the next day, entirely on account of this concentrated twelve-hours work and exceptional memory, I read the entire page without missing a word. . . . Of course this was exceptional; but it shows what concentration of mind will do. Going on in read Caesar it took me almost a day to realize definitely just how great Caesar really was. This was to me great inspiration, and that year, in addition to keeping up my Latin, I had learned, or was learning, in a self-taught way, German, Greek, mathematics, and composition. Since then I have been longing for theught from the Savoy teachers.
